explain.say: The internet is like a giant city full of amazing places: games, videos and facts about dinosaurs. And just like in a real city, a few simple rules keep you safe. Look at the board: five rules, and we will tick them off together.

explain.say: Rule one: keep your details private. Your full name, your address, your school and your passwords are like the keys to your home. Would you hand your house key to a stranger in the street?

explain.say: Amara stopped and asked, so she stayed safe. Now look at rule four: never meet strangers. Someone you meet in a game may not be who they say. Never agree to meet them without a grown-up. Who are the grown-ups you could tell?

faq.q: What personal information should I keep private?
faq.a: Keep private your full name, home address, school, phone number, passwords and photos that show where you live or go to school. Ask a grown-up before sharing anything about yourself.
asks: What should I not share online?
Is it safe to tell people my school?

faq.q: What should I do if something online upsets me?
faq.a: Stop, do not reply, and tell an adult you trust, like a parent, carer or teacher. You can close the screen, and you will not be in trouble for telling.
asks: What do I do if something online scares me?
Who should I tell about something bad online?

faq.q: What if someone online wants to meet me?
faq.a: Never agree to meet someone you only know online without a parent or carer. Tell a trusted adult straight away, because people online are not always who they say.
asks: Is it safe to meet online friends?
Someone in a game asked to meet me

faq.q: Are pop-ups that say I won a prize real?
faq.a: Almost never. They are tricks to get your details or put a virus on the device. Do not click them; show a grown-up instead.
asks: Did I really win a prize?

faq.q: How can I be kind online?
faq.a: Only post or send what you would happily say to someone's face. If you see someone being unkind, do not join in, and tell a trusted adult.

facts: Safer Internet Day is held each February and is marked in more than 180 countries.
Many apps, including most social media, set 13 as the minimum age to have an account.

quiz.say: A message in a game asks which school you go to. What should you do?
quiz.show: Someone asks for your school. You…

options.show: Tell them, it is only a game
options.say: Tell them, it is only a game

options.show: Do not answer and tell a grown-up
options.say: Do not answer and tell a grown-up

quiz.why: Your school is private information, and a trusted adult can help you deal with the message.

wrong.0: People in games can use your school to find you in real life.
wrong.2: A photo can show even more about where you are.

quiz.say: Who should you tell if something online makes you feel scared?
quiz.show: If something online scares you, tell…
quiz.why: A parent, carer or teacher can help, and you will not be in trouble.

wrong.1: Keeping it secret means no one can help you.
wrong.2: Do not reply to them; tell a trusted adult instead.
